blocks.text: The letter came with wind, and the wind at home, that afternoon, changed its mind too. It was a levante, a real one, the local kind: the Mar Menor stood up all at once, the sky came down to the roof tiles, a rush-seat chair rolled across to the wall. Andrés, who had gone out at dawn (“I'll be back before the weather closes in”), heard the words like an echo of himself from a distant year, and didn't know whether he had just said them or was remembering them, or whether the other one was saying them, in a world where a gale was also breaking loose at that hour.

blocks.text: Because over there, on a planet with a dark coast and a sky that was far too low, the clone was in a small vessel, not six metres long but a working boat all the same, and the water had turned opaque and heavy, and there was no shore in sight. The bridge, instead of bringing one scene after another, joined the two. The rain of Lo Pagán and the rain of that sea soaked Andrés through the same shirt. The engine of his boat and the engine of the other mingled in his ear. A flash of lightning here was a flash of lightning there. The fear was one and the same.

blocks.text: Aya, on land, stayed on the doorstep, in a coat that was no longer the one from 2060 and yet was, in the business of getting wet. She didn't notify anyone. There was no Nexum protocol to turn to any more, and she wouldn't have called it in any case. She looked at the angry plate, the bent reeds, and thought, with an exactness that hurt, of the first storm, of the four hours, of the clock that ran two minutes slow, of the coffee made again. Now the man didn't grow old, the boat was the same, and she, once again, was waiting.

blocks.text: On the water, Andrés couldn't tell things apart. The rope was cutting his palm, or the other's, or both. The taste of salt was the taste of home and, at times, of that metallic fig from the second world, as if all the seas he had received were converging on this single hour. He said Aya's name, and so did the clone, and the bridge, for the first time, was not a letter from one to the other but a room: both of them, at once, in the same storm, looking at each other not with their eyes but with the shared memory of an afternoon when the levante shook this plate and a woman didn't notify anyone, and a man came back.

blocks.text: “Who are you?” asked Andrés, or the other, or both.
blocks.html: “Who are you?” asked Andrés, or the other, or both.

blocks.text: “You,” said the other mouth. “Me. The one who stayed. The one who searches. I don't know how to finish the list.”

blocks.text: A wave, here or there, lifted them. There was no shipwreck. There was, though, an instant in which the man from Lo Pagán didn't know whether he was six metres from his shore or a lifetime away from it, and he closed his eyes, and saw the doorstep, and the cup, and Lía as a girl on the Moon, and Lía as a woman at the plot, and Vicente, and the ship crossing the sky, and he said, not to resolve anything, but to moor himself:

There was, though, an instant in which the man from Lo Pagán didn't know whether he was six metres from his shore or a lifetime away from it, and he closed his eyes, and saw the doorstep, and the cup, and Lía as a girl on the Moon, and Lía as a woman at the plot, and Vicente, and the ship crossing the sky, and he said, not to resolve anything, but to moor himself:

blocks.text: “One to stay and one to search. That's what we said. I'm staying. Even if right now I don't know what water I'm in. I'm staying.”

blocks.text: The clone, in his own storm, answered with the same words turned inside out, which is another way of being faithful:
blocks.html: The clone, in his own storm, answered with the same words turned inside out, which is another way of being faithful:

blocks.text: “I'm searching. Even though right now I feel you so close I could ask for the shore. I won't ask for it. I'll write to you. That's what I can give you.”
blocks.html: “I'm searching. Even though right now I feel you so close I could ask for the shore. I won't ask for it. I'll write to you. That's what I can give you.”

blocks.text: Little by little, the two storms came apart from each other, the way two nets that have become tangled come apart when a fisherman patiently undoes them. The levante at home began to tire. The one over there did too, or the letter moved away, or both. Andrés at last saw the promenade, the house, Aya's figure in the doorway, the wet coat, and steered the boat toward her with the precision of someone returning not only from fishing but from a mirror.

blocks.text: He arrived soaked, whole, with a new line across his palm, his own, from this water. Aya received him without reproach, sat him down, gave him a towel, the coffee, the half minute, and didn't question him straight away. Lía came running from the plot, her hair plastered to her face, because the harbour, in her hand, had lit up like a warning.

blocks.text: “I've seen both,” said Andrés, when his voice came back. “Both storms. The one from back then and the one from now, the one here and the one over there. I didn't know which one was soaking me. I knew when I saw her, you, Aya, on the doorstep. That belonged to this world. The rest, I wouldn't swear to.”

blocks.text: Lía sat on the floor at his feet, as when she was little and the module on the Moon never quite became home. This time she didn't ask in a little girl's voice. She asked in her usual one, the one the grandmothers had taught her, and the question was the one from the night of the ship, given back, not out of cruelty but out of need:

She asked in her usual one, the one the grandmothers had taught her, and the question was the one from the night of the ship, given back, not out of cruelty but out of need:

blocks.text: “If you've both been in the same storm, which of you is my father?”
blocks.html: “If you've both been in the same storm, which of you is my father?”

blocks.text: Andrés looked at her. There was water on her eyelashes, from the rain, or from something else.
blocks.html: Andrés looked at her. There was water on her eyelashes, from the rain, or from something else.

blocks.text: “Both,” he said again. “And if you want a slower answer, I'll give you one: the one talking to you now is the one from this shore. The one who remembers you on the Moon and writes to you from a water I've never set foot in is too. Today, on the bridge, we met. We didn't merge. That was what mattered. The chorus taught me that. The forest did too. I'm the one who comes back to this towel. He's the one who carries on. You're the one who asks us, so that we don't forget.”

blocks.text: Aya, with a hand on each of their shoulders, added (and there was Eva in her tone, not to dictate but to open):

blocks.text: *If a storm is shared, does it stop belonging to anyone? Or does it become, precisely then, the property of those who went through it together, even if one of them never left his own sea?*

blocks.text: MAY, without judgment, the fact:
blocks.html: MAY, without judgment, the fact:

blocks.text: *Two storms have coincided in one memory. A man has come back to a door. The other has not asked for the shore. The daughter has repeated her question. Those are the things that happened this afternoon.*

blocks.text: Outside, the wind was dropping. The Mar Menor, being so enclosed, has no open-sea swell, and yet it knows how to calm down with the same ugly haste with which it loses its temper. The rush-seat chair stayed by the wall. Nobody picked it up straight away. They let the house smell of rain and coffee, which is a real smell, the kind a forest never quite manages to copy.

He looked, if anything, for a place where a young man, with his very memory and a different boat, refused to ask for this shore and yet loved it. He spoke to him, not aloud but through the bridge, which was still vibrating, like a net just untangled:
blocks.html: Later, Andrés looked out into the courtyard and up at the sky. He didn't look for the ship. He looked, if anything, for a place where a young man, with his very memory and a different boat, refused to ask for this shore and yet loved it. He spoke to him, not aloud but through the bridge, which was still vibrating, like a net just untangled:

blocks.text: “Thank you for not asking me for the doorstep. And I thank myself for not asking you for the journey. Keep writing. I'll keep reading. And if one day the storms come together again, I know now which door to look at.”

blocks.text: There was no answering voice. There was, barely, a sense of agreement, a rope held fast on the other side. Lía, from the kitchen, said his name once, as they had agreed, so that the edge would stay where it belonged.
